lessons.title: Shock protection
lessons.summary: {Term:shock-protection-device} protection cuts the power in a fraction of a second when current leaks to earth through a person or through water, which limits the harm. It does not help if someone touches both live wires.
whatToLookFor: Outlets near water: sinks, tubs, showers, pools and outdoor taps
Outdoors, garages, basements, crawl spaces and laundry areas, where floors and walls are often damp
A TEST and RESET button on the {term:receptacle} or the {term:breaker}
Outlets further along the same circuit: are they covered by the protection too?
lessons.whyItMatters: Even a small current through the body can be deadly, and wet skin and damp floors let far more current flow than dry ones.

tiers.foundation: Recognise the places that need protection and spot an outlet that has none.
tiers.practitioner: Work out which outlets need protection where you are (in some regions almost all of them) and how it is provided: a device at the outlet, or at the {term:breaker}.
tiers.authority: Handle the edge cases: shared circuits, appliances, new and replaced outlets, and confirming that the protection actually works.

commonMistakes: Assuming a protected outlet nearby covers the whole room
Forgetting indoor damp places such as basements and utility areas
Treating arc-fault protection and ground-fault protection as the same thing
Believing it protects against touching two live wires at once

lessons.title: Arc-fault protection
lessons.summary: {Term:arc-fault-device} protection detects the sparking of damaged or loose wiring, which an ordinary {term:breaker} cannot see, and cuts the power before it starts a fire.
whatToLookFor: Which rooms and circuits need this protection where you are
A test button on the {term:breaker}, or an outlet-type device further along the circuit
Circuits that were extended or changed after they were first wired
Protection that only guards against ground faults, which does not count
lessons.whyItMatters: Arcing can heat wiring and the material around it enough to start a fire without ever overloading the circuit, so an ordinary breaker may never trip.

tiers.foundation: Recognise where arc-fault protection is required and spot a circuit with only a plain {term:breaker}.
tiers.practitioner: Tell which circuits need it and which ways of providing it are acceptable.
tiers.authority: Handle changes to existing circuits, replaced devices and the limits on how far an outlet-type device can sit from the {term:panel}.

commonMistakes: Counting a ground-fault device as arc-fault protection
Forgetting that a changed or extended circuit can bring the new rules with it
Overlooking closets, hallways and other rooms that look unimportant

lessons.title: Overcurrent protection
lessons.summary: A {term:breaker} or fuse is the safety valve for the wire behind it: it must trip before the wire gets hot enough to be damaged.
whatToLookFor: The rating of each {term:breaker} compared with the size of the wire it protects
Breakers that must switch off together but are not tied together
Fuses of the wrong kind or size, and bare fuse sockets that accept any size
Ratings and markings on the {term:panel}, and a main device that is too large for the panel
lessons.whyItMatters: If the protection is larger than the wire can carry, the wire can overheat and start a fire long before the {term:breaker} trips.

tiers.foundation: Recognise what a {term:breaker} protects and spot an obvious mismatch between its rating and the wire.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the usual rules for small wire, tied handles, fuses and panel ratings.
tiers.authority: Handle taps, series ratings, switching duty and the cases where the general rule has an exception.

commonMistakes: Raising a {term:breaker} size to stop it tripping instead of finding the cause
Sizing the protection to the appliance and forgetting the wire
Assuming two breakers side by side are tied together

lessons.title: Conductor sizing
lessons.summary: A wire must be thick enough for the current it carries, once heat, bundling and its surroundings are taken into account.
whatToLookFor: The wire size on a circuit compared with the {term:breaker} and the load
Many wires bundled together in one conduit or cable, which cannot shed heat as well
Hot places such as attics, boiler rooms and sunny roofs
The temperature rating of the terminals, and whether the wire is copper or aluminium
Loads that run for hours, such as chargers and heaters
lessons.whyItMatters: A thin wire carrying too much current heats up, damages its insulation and can start a fire, and the damage is often hidden inside a wall.

tiers.foundation: Read a wire size and spot a wire that is obviously too small for its {term:breaker}.
tiers.practitioner: Use the ampacity tables with the common corrections for bundling, heat and terminals.
tiers.authority: Size feeders and services, handle parallel runs, nonlinear loads and aluminium, and explain where the table value cannot be used.

commonMistakes: Using the highest table value without checking what the terminals allow
Forgetting to reduce the rating for many wires in one conduit
Ignoring a hot location

lessons.title: Grounding and bonding
lessons.summary: {Term:grounding} and bonding give fault current an easy path back to the source so a {term:breaker} trips, and keep metal parts from staying live.
whatToLookFor: The connection between the {term:panel} and the earth: an electrode or the supplier's earth terminal, and the wire that joins them
Metal water and gas pipes bonded to the system
The neutral and the ground joined at one place only, normally the service
Metal parts that could become live in a fault: enclosures, conduit, appliance frames
Clamps, splices and connections that could loosen or corrode
lessons.whyItMatters: Without a good path for fault current, a live metal part can stay dangerous for anyone who touches it and the {term:breaker} may never trip.

tiers.foundation: Tell the neutral from the ground and spot a missing connection to a pipe or electrode.
tiers.practitioner: Check the {term:grounding} connections, bonding of pipes and the sizing of the main conductors.
tiers.authority: Handle separately derived systems, extra electrodes, splices and special equipment.

commonMistakes: Confusing the neutral with the ground, or joining them at a subpanel
Assuming a {term:ground-rod} alone makes the system safe
Skipping the bonding of metal piping

lessons.title: Branch circuit requirements
lessons.summary: Branch circuit rules decide how many circuits a building needs and where outlets must go, so cords do not stretch across rooms and no circuit is overloaded.
whatToLookFor: How the circuits are divided so heavy loads have their own
Outlet spacing and counts along walls and countertops, where the rules set them
Outlets in hallways, outdoors and in garages, where the rules require them
Outlets mounted too high or too low to count toward a requirement
A {term:receptacle} near heating and cooling equipment, where required for servicing
lessons.whyItMatters: Too few outlets lead to extension cords and overloaded circuits, which are a common cause of home fires.

tiers.foundation: Spot a room or area with no outlet or an outlet in an unusable place.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the spacing and count rules to a floor plan and check the circuits that serve each room.
tiers.authority: Handle islands, peninsulas, special appliances, and local amendments to the model rules.

commonMistakes: Assuming a room with a single outlet is fine because it is small
Counting an outlet that is mounted too high or too low
Forgetting the garage, outdoors and the laundry area

lessons.title: Load calculation
lessons.summary: A load calculation works out how much power a building can draw so the service, feeders and breakers are big enough.
whatToLookFor: The size of the service compared with the calculated load
Large loads such as ranges, dryers, heat pumps and chargers
Loads that run continuously, which count for more
Demand factors: not every load runs at once
Loads that were added after the original design
lessons.whyItMatters: A service that is too small trips, overheats or cannot take new equipment, and a calculation that is too generous wastes money.

tiers.foundation: List the loads in a building and tell which ones need special treatment.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the standard steps for a house or a small building, including demand factors.
tiers.authority: Handle additions, special loads and the rules that treat some loads differently.

commonMistakes: Adding every load at full value and ignoring demand factors
Forgetting a load that runs for hours
Not recalculating when a large load is added

lessons.title: Disconnecting means
lessons.summary: Disconnects let someone shut power off quickly and safely, so they must be where people can find and reach them.
whatToLookFor: The main shut-off for the building: where it is and whether you can reach it
Equipment that needs its own disconnect within sight, such as an air conditioner or a motor
How many main disconnects there are, and whether they are grouped
Disconnects that are hidden, blocked, too high, or cannot be locked off
Labels that say what each disconnect controls
lessons.whyItMatters: In an emergency or while servicing equipment, seconds matter, and a disconnect that cannot be found or reached is useless.

tiers.foundation: Find the main disconnect and spot one that is blocked or missing.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the rules on location, number, sight lines and marking.
tiers.authority: Handle outbuildings, groups of disconnects, lockout provisions and equipment with special rules.

commonMistakes: Putting the shut-off where it can only be reached by moving stored items
Assuming a {term:breaker} in a distant {term:panel} is enough without checking where the rules allow it
Forgetting to label what each disconnect controls

lessons.title: Working space and access
lessons.summary: Panels and other equipment need clear, lit space around them so a person can work safely and get away quickly.
whatToLookFor: Storage, shelves, or appliances in front of a {term:panel}
Enough width, depth and headroom in front of the equipment
Panels in places the rules restrict, such as bathrooms, near stored combustibles, or over stairs
The {term:panel} door: can it open fully?
Pipes, ducts and other systems above the {term:panel}
lessons.whyItMatters: A person working on live equipment needs room to move and a clear way out, because an arc flash or shock can make them fall or recoil.

tiers.foundation: Spot stored items or a blocked door at a {term:panel}.
tiers.practitioner: Check the clear width, depth, headroom and a suitable location.
tiers.authority: Handle the reserved space above equipment, lighting, access by ladder or stairs, and the special cases that change the rules.

commonMistakes: Treating a floor marking as enough when the space above is blocked
Putting a {term:panel} somewhere awkward because there was spare wall
Forgetting the space must stay clear for as long as the equipment is there

lessons.title: Equipment installation
lessons.summary: Good workmanship keeps connections tight, enclosures closed and parts undamaged, so equipment stays safe for years.
whatToLookFor: Open holes in an enclosure, and cables that enter without a clamp or connector
A loose or unsecured {term:panel} or box
Loose or overcrowded terminals, and more than one wire under a screw that is meant for one
Damaged parts: cracked covers, nicked wires and paint on terminals
Missing covers, dead fronts or filler pieces
lessons.whyItMatters: Poor connections are one of the most common causes of electrical fires and failures.

tiers.foundation: Spot open holes, loose covers and damaged parts.
tiers.practitioner: Check how cables are secured, how terminals are loaded, and that enclosures are complete.
tiers.authority: Judge subtle damage, workmanship that looks fine but breaks a rule, and how a repair should be made.

commonMistakes: Judging workmanship by how tidy it looks instead of how it is secured
Putting two wires under one terminal without checking it allows it
Leaving a dead front off to make servicing easier

lessons.title: Identification and marking
lessons.summary: Clear labels tell the next person what each circuit and disconnect controls and what the equipment is rated for.
whatToLookFor: A circuit directory at the {term:panel} that names what each circuit serves
Disconnects and {term:service-disconnect} devices that say what they are
Labels that are faded, vague, or use a person's name instead of a place or load
Ratings and nameplates on equipment, and a label where a special rating is relied on
Markings that are permanent and easy to read
lessons.whyItMatters: In a fault or an emergency, a person may need to shut off one circuit fast, and a wrong or missing label sends them to the wrong place.

tiers.foundation: Notice a {term:panel} with no directory or an unlabelled disconnect.
tiers.practitioner: Check that labels are specific, accurate and durable.
tiers.authority: Handle special markings, series ratings and changes made after the first labelling.

commonMistakes: Writing room names that do not tell you which circuit is which
Letting a directory go out of date after changes
Labelling a device with a handwritten note that fades

lessons.title: Wiring methods
lessons.summary: Cable and conduit must be chosen for the place and installed so they are supported, protected and joined in accessible boxes.
whatToLookFor: Cable that is unsupported, stapled too tightly, or bent too sharply
Cable exposed where it can be damaged, or passing through framing with no protection
Splices outside a box, covers missing, or boxes buried behind a finished wall
Conduit that is not supported, or plastic conduit with no allowance for movement
Wiring in a wet, buried or outdoor location with the wrong type of cable
lessons.whyItMatters: Damaged, unsupported or hidden wiring causes faults and fires, and a buried splice cannot be inspected or repaired.

tiers.foundation: Spot unsupported cable, a missing cover and a splice outside a box.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the support, protection, bending and box rules for the common wiring methods.
tiers.authority: Choose a method for a difficult location and judge subtle faults such as box position and expansion.

commonMistakes: Using the same method indoors and outdoors without checking the location
Burying a junction box behind a finished surface
Forgetting that plastic conduit grows and shrinks with temperature

lessons.title: Special locations
lessons.summary: Pools, spas, charging stations, generators and similar places have extra rules because water, vehicles or a second power source make the usual protection not enough.
whatToLookFor: Pools and spas: outlet distances, bonding of metal parts, light heights and where the disconnect is
Overhead lines near a pool or a structure
Weatherproof covers and protection on outdoor outlets
Charging equipment: its disconnect, protection and mounting
A standby generator and how it is connected, so it cannot send power back to the grid
lessons.whyItMatters: These places combine electricity with water, people in bare feet or a power source the utility does not control, so mistakes are more dangerous.

tiers.foundation: Recognise a special location and spot a missing cover or an obviously wrong distance.
tiers.practitioner: Apply the distance, bonding and protection rules for the common special locations.
tiers.authority: Handle the interaction between a special location's rules and the general rules, and equipment that is new to the code.

commonMistakes: Treating a poolside outlet like any other outdoor outlet
Forgetting to bond metal parts near water
Connecting a generator in a way that can back-feed the building

lessons.title: Electrically safe work
lessons.summary: Making a circuit or piece of equipment safe to work on, and proving it is dead, before anyone touches it.
whatToLookFor: Every source of power to the equipment, including a second feed or a generator that could send power back
The disconnect or {term:breaker} that isolates it, and whether it can be locked and tagged
A personal lock and tag on each isolation point, removed only by the person who put it there
A meter that is proved on a known live source before and after it tests the circuit
Stored energy that can remain after the power is off, such as a capacitor or a spring
lessons.whyItMatters: A wrong belief that a circuit is dead is behind many serious electrical injuries, and proving it dead is the step that stops them.

tiers.foundation: Name the steps of making a circuit safe and spot work being done on live parts without them.
tiers.practitioner: Carry out the sequence in order: identify the sources, isolate, lock and tag, test with a proved meter, then work.
tiers.authority: Plan the procedure for complex equipment: several sources, group lockout, stored energy, and when work on live parts is justified and what protection it needs.

commonMistakes: Trusting a switch position or a label instead of testing
Testing with a meter that was not first proved on a known live source
Removing a lock that belongs to someone else
Forgetting that a second source can still feed the equipment

lessons.title: Testing and measurement
lessons.summary: Choosing and using a meter or tester correctly and reading what it shows, so you know what is really happening in a circuit.
whatToLookFor: Which tester suits the job: a voltage tester, a continuity tester, a {term:receptacle} tester, an insulation tester
The meter's rating, its leads and their condition
The test points: between which conductors you are measuring
A reading that does not match what you expect, and what that says about the circuit
The test button on a {term:shock-protection-device} or {term:arc-fault-device}, which proves that it trips
lessons.whyItMatters: A measurement is only as good as the instrument and the way it is used, and a wrong choice can give a false reading or put the person at risk.

tiers.foundation: Name the common testers and what each is for.
tiers.practitioner: Choose the right tester, connect it correctly and read the result for a finished circuit.
tiers.authority: Design a test plan for an installation, interpret unexpected readings, and know a tester's limits.

commonMistakes: Using a meter set to the wrong function for the job
Trusting a tester that was not itself checked
Measuring continuity on a circuit that is still live
Reading a result without asking whether it makes sense

lessons.title: Troubleshooting
lessons.summary: Finding the cause of a dead or tripping circuit by narrowing it down step by step instead of guessing.
whatToLookFor: What changed: new loads, recent work, damage or weather
Whether the problem is the supply, the protection device or the load
Splitting the circuit in half to see which half holds the fault
A device that trips again when it is reset, which means the fault is still there
Signs of heat or damage at connections
lessons.whyItMatters: Guessing wastes time and can leave a dangerous fault in place; a method finds the cause safely and fixes it.

tiers.foundation: Describe the symptoms and say which part of the circuit could be at fault.
tiers.practitioner: Follow a method to isolate a fault in a branch circuit, using the safe-work and testing steps.
tiers.authority: Handle intermittent and multiple faults, and decide when a problem is beyond the circuit and needs a different expert.

commonMistakes: Resetting a tripped device again and again
Replacing parts before finding the cause
Working on the circuit before making it safe
Stopping at the first fault found without checking for a second

lessons.title: Plans and documentation
lessons.summary: Reading drawings, schedules and diagrams, laying out work from them, and recording what was found or done.
whatToLookFor: The symbols and the legend on a drawing
A {term:panel} schedule that matches what is installed
Dimensions, and where equipment must go
Notes and revisions: is this the latest version?
Records: inspection notes, test results and correction notices
lessons.whyItMatters: Many mistakes in the field start with a drawing that was misread or a finding that was never written down.

tiers.foundation: Read the symbols and find a circuit or device on a simple drawing.
tiers.practitioner: Lay out work from drawings and keep accurate records of what was installed, tested or found.
tiers.authority: Review plans and schedules for completeness and conflicts, and write findings that others can act on.

commonMistakes: Working from an old version of a drawing
Assuming a schedule is right without checking the installation
Writing a finding without the place, the problem and what must change

lessons.title: Jobsite safety
lessons.summary: The general hazards of the job apart from electricity: ladders and falls, tools and cords, materials, enclosed spaces and a tidy site.
whatToLookFor: A ladder set up on firm ground at a safe angle, with non-conductive rails near electrical work
Tools and cords in good condition, with ground-fault protection where it is needed
Heights: edges, roofs and lifts, and the fall protection in use
Enclosed spaces and trenches, and how people get out
Materials stored and handled so that no one trips or is struck
A pre-job briefing that names the hazards and who is responsible
lessons.whyItMatters: Falls and tool injuries are common on electrical jobs, and the person who has just made the circuit safe can still be hurt by the ladder.

tiers.foundation: Spot the common hazards on a jobsite and say what protection is needed.
tiers.practitioner: Set up and inspect a ladder and tools, choose protection for heights and keep the site clear.
tiers.authority: Plan a job's hazards and controls, brief the crew and stop work when conditions change.

commonMistakes: Using a metal ladder near live parts
Skipping the pre-job briefing because the job is small
Leaving cords and materials where people walk

lessons.title: Code administration
lessons.summary: How the code is adopted and enforced: which edition applies, the stages of a permit and inspection, and what an inspector does with what they find.
whatToLookFor: Which edition and which local changes apply where the work is
The permit and the inspection stages: work must be seen before it is covered
What an inspector checks at each stage
How a correction is recorded and how work is approved or rejected
Who has the authority to decide a doubtful case
lessons.whyItMatters: The same installation can be right in one place and wrong in another because the rules adopted differ, and knowing the process avoids rework and keeps hidden work inspectable.

tiers.foundation: Describe why work is permitted and inspected and name the usual stages.
tiers.practitioner: Prepare work for each inspection stage and respond to a correction notice.
tiers.authority: Check the adopted edition and local amendments, review plans, decide approval or rejection and record the reasons.

commonMistakes: Covering work before it is inspected
Assuming the newest edition applies everywhere
Treating a correction notice as a suggestion

lessons.title: Utility interface
lessons.summary: Where the utility's equipment ends and the customer's begins: the service point, the meter, and the connections made there.
whatToLookFor: The service point and who owns what on each side of it
The meter socket and the service entrance equipment
The {term:grounding} and bonding connections at the service
The {term:service-disconnect} near where the service enters
What only the utility may touch, such as the meter seal and the utility's conductors
lessons.whyItMatters: Work on the wrong side of the service point can be unsafe and unlawful, and the rules that apply change at that point.

tiers.foundation: Point out the service point and say which side belongs to the customer.
tiers.practitioner: Check the customer-side service equipment and its connections, and coordinate a shut-off and reconnection with the utility.
tiers.authority: Handle changes and upgrades at the service, including grounding, metering and the rules that differ between utilities.

commonMistakes: Working on a utility conductor or breaking a meter seal
Assuming the rules on the line side are the same as on the customer side
Forgetting to arrange the utility's shut-off before starting
